projects.title: One engine. Many connectors.
projects.outcome: Turning connector-specific forms into a reusable, schema-driven product system.
projects.problem: Every new cloud connector brought another configuration form, another collection of conditional fields, and another opportunity for behavior to drift. The challenge was to make a growing set of integrations understandable without maintaining a separate interface for every variant.
constraints: A mature Vue 2 platform with existing customers and established workflows.
Backend metadata could arrive partially populated or differ between service versions.
Field dependencies, visibility, defaults, and validation had to remain consistent.

decisions.title: Make the contract describe the interface.
decisions.body: Go and Python services supplied JSON metadata for field types, defaults, validation, dependencies, and conditional visibility. The Vue layer interpreted that contract into reusable rendering behavior.

decisions.title: Normalize before rendering.
decisions.body: A stable UI-facing model absorbed missing metadata and version differences. Backward-compatible defaults kept partial responses from becoming broken forms.

decisions.title: Keep conditions and errors in one place.
decisions.body: Centralized condition evaluation and field-level validation mapping replaced scattered connector-specific fixes. The same rules informed what appeared and what could be submitted.

projects.contribution: I owned the frontend workstream and connector configuration re-architecture, coordinated service contracts with Go/Python engineers, reviewed implementation decisions, and guided delivery with product and QA.
projects.impact: Configuration logic became reusable across connector variants. Normalization and centralized rules reduced duplicated behavior and made new variants safer to introduce.
projects.reflection: The next useful improvement is a versioned contract fixture suite: representative service responses that exercise dependencies and partial-metadata behavior before a release.
projects.confidentiality: Public-safe reconstruction based on my CV. No customer data, internal screenshots, or production topology.

projects.title: Make the waiting make sense.
projects.outcome: Predictable interfaces for long-running scans, cancellation, recovery, and service state.
projects.role: Software Development Engineer → Senior Software Engineer
projects.problem: A long-running operation is more than a spinner. Service responses, permissions, cancellation requests, and stale client state can disagree. People need to know what is happening and what action is safe to take next.
constraints: Asynchronous jobs with independently changing backend state.
Multiple integrations and inconsistent service status responses.
Existing permissions, filters, pagination, and release constraints.

decisions.title: Give every meaningful state a name.
decisions.body: Loading, partial data, retry, cancellation, failure, and terminal outcomes became explicit states. State normalization gave Vuex a consistent model of service behavior.

decisions.title: Trace the whole path.
decisions.body: Production debugging followed browser behavior through Vue/Vuex updates, API payloads, and Go/Python responses. Fixes went into the layer where the failure actually originated.

decisions.title: Treat recovery as a product feature.
decisions.body: Permission-denied, empty, partial, and backend-error states were implemented as intentional user experiences instead of being left outside the happy path.

projects.contribution: I implemented and debugged discovery status and cancellation, catalog filtering, scope and permissions, export, and related enterprise workflows. I aligned contracts and verified regressions with backend and QA teams.
projects.impact: Long-running operations became more understandable and recoverable. Explicit state paths reduced stale and inconsistent behavior across integration screens.
projects.reflection: I would extend deterministic scenario testing around delayed responses, cancellation races, and permission changes during an active job.
projects.confidentiality: A simplified account of publicly shareable engineering work. Internal data and endpoints are omitted.

projects.title: A faster path forward.
projects.outcome: A compatibility-first Rsbuild/Rspack proof of concept for an established Vue 2 platform.
projects.problem: Legacy build tooling creates friction well beyond compilation. Changing it can affect asynchronous imports, routing, assets, development workflows, and production delivery. The goal was to evaluate a better path without destabilizing the application.
constraints: An established Vue 2 application on Webpack 4.
Existing route, asset, and async import behavior had to remain compatible.
Docker/Kubernetes environments and release verification added constraints beyond a local build.

decisions.title: Prove compatibility before promising migration.
decisions.body: I led a Rsbuild/Rspack proof of concept around the existing application. Runtime behavior, routing, asset handling, and async imports were explicit validation targets.

decisions.title: Test the environment as well as the code.
decisions.body: Build and deployment checks covered environment-specific behavior and regression risks, with smoke verification and release troubleshooting supporting confidence.

decisions.title: Keep the change surface small.
decisions.body: The effort focused on a lower-risk modernization path around the existing product rather than requiring a simultaneous framework rewrite.

projects.contribution: I led the bundler compatibility proof of concept and supported build validation, deployment checks, regression fixes, and release verification.
projects.impact: The proof of concept established a lower-risk path for modernizing a legacy build system. It is presented as compatibility work, with no unverified speedup or production migration claims.
projects.reflection: A next iteration should publish repeatable cold-build, incremental-build, and runtime baselines across identical environments before selecting the final rollout strategy.
projects.confidentiality: Architecture is deliberately simplified. This work was a proof of concept, not a claimed completed production migration.

posts.title: A 3D portfolio should still work without 3D.
posts.excerpt: The most important layer in an immersive experience is the one that loads before the canvas.
posts.mdx:
## The first render is a product decision

The Kinetic Garden begins as an HTML page. The name, positioning, selected work, and CV navigation do not wait for a renderer. That order matters: the visitor came to understand the work, and the canvas is one way to explore it.

A WebGL context can fail. A GPU can be busy. A visitor may prefer reduced motion. None of those conditions should remove access to a case study.

## A boundary around the experience

The public pages use Astro. A React island contains the interactive scene, and the scene module is loaded separately. The reading route uses the same content records but does not import the world.

```tsx
const World = lazy(() => import('./World'));

// The semantic portfolio has already rendered.
<Suspense fallback={null}>
  <World quality={quality} preferences={preferences} />
</Suspense>
```

The scene has two failure boundaries: capability detection before initialization, and an error boundary around the mounted world. Context loss also needs handling after the renderer has started. A loading check alone does not cover it.

## Make the alternate path useful

Reading mode is a deliberate route with a compact profile, experience, work, skills, and CV actions. It is not an error message. It should be the fastest path for someone who wants to evaluate the engineering rather than explore the sculpture.

## What still needs measurement

A split bundle is an architectural choice, not proof of speed. Production verification needs to inspect the actual network waterfall, measure the critical route, and check representative devices. A beautiful desktop render is not a substitute for that evidence.

posts.title: The interface is only half the state machine.
posts.excerpt: A practical model for making long-running work, cancellation, and recovery understandable.
posts.mdx:
## A boolean cannot explain a long-running job

Loading is often introduced as a boolean. That works until an operation can be queued, running, partially complete, cancelling, cancelled, or failed. When several booleans describe those conditions independently, impossible combinations become representable.

The following example is a conceptual model, not production code from an employer.

```ts
type JobState =
  | { kind: 'idle' }
  | { kind: 'running'; jobId: string }
  | { kind: 'cancelling'; jobId: string }
  | { kind: 'complete'; resultId: string }
  | { kind: 'cancelled' }
  | { kind: 'failed'; retryable: boolean };
```

## Normalize at the service boundary

Different integrations may return different status names or incomplete payloads. A normalization layer should map supported responses to the model the UI understands. Unknown states deserve an explicit treatment; silently treating them as success is dangerous.

Normalization does not mean hiding uncertainty. If the service does not provide a completion estimate, the interface should not invent a precise percentage.

## Cancellation is a request, not an outcome

A user pressing Cancel does not prove the job has stopped. The interface can acknowledge the request immediately while keeping a separate cancelling state until the service confirms a terminal result.

The same distinction applies to retry. A retry action may fail before a new operation starts. Clear transitions prevent a spinner from becoming the only record of what happened.

## Test disagreement

Useful test cases include a delayed response from an earlier request, a permission change during work, a cancellation that races with completion, and a partial response missing expected metadata.

These cases force an engineering team to decide which source is authoritative and when the UI should show uncertainty. That decision is part of the product, not an afterthought for error handling.

posts.title: Modernize the build. Keep the product steady.
posts.excerpt: Why a tooling proof of concept should be designed around compatibility, not a headline speedup.
posts.mdx:
## Start with the contract the product already relies on

A mature application relies on far more than a successful compilation. It expects particular asset URLs, route behavior, module loading, environment configuration, and deployment output. A new bundler has to preserve those expectations or change them deliberately.

## Build a compatibility inventory

For a migration proof of concept, the useful checklist includes dynamic imports, route entry points, styles, static assets, development behavior, and production runtime checks. Each item should have a reproducible example and an expected result.

```text
Existing application
  → dependency compatibility
  → import and asset behavior
  → route and runtime smoke checks
  → production output
  → deployment verification
```

## Separate the questions

Does it build? Does it behave correctly? Does it improve developer experience? Can the team operate it? Those are separate questions. A positive answer to the first should not be presented as evidence for all four.

Performance comparisons also require a repeatable environment. Cold builds, incremental builds, and browser runtime are different measurements. An attractive number without those conditions is not a useful decision aid.

## Keep rollback understandable

A smaller change surface makes it easier to isolate a regression and return to the previous path. Combining a bundler change with a framework rewrite may be justified, but it also makes it harder to identify which change caused a failure.

The modernization project described in this portfolio is a compatibility proof of concept. It does not claim a completed production migration or an unverified percentage improvement. That boundary is part of telling the engineering story accurately.

hero.description: I connect interfaces, APIs, data, and delivery to build reliable products—and design clear paths for them to grow.

about.teaser: I like the problems that look simple from the outside and have ten moving parts underneath.
about.summary: I’ve spent 5+ years working where interfaces, backend services, and product expectations meet. Sometimes that means untangling state. Sometimes it means tracing a failure across the stack. Always, it means making the result easier for someone else to use.

sections.title: Start with the whole picture.
paragraphs: I’m Salman, a full-stack engineer with a strong frontend foundation. The work I enjoy most sits between product behavior, service contracts, state, and the small interface details that make a difficult workflow feel obvious.

My path has taken me from startup React products and React Native apps to enterprise privacy and data-security systems. Along the way, I’ve learned that a reliable interface starts well before the component: in the contract, the state model, the failure paths, and the decisions about what happens next.

sections.title: Fix the cause. Keep the system clear.
paragraphs: When a production issue crosses several layers, I follow it. That can mean tracing Vuex state, checking an API payload, working through a Go or Python service response, or investigating a difference in a deployment environment.

I like architecture that a team can keep working with. Reusable patterns, explicit state, and a smaller change surface are often more valuable than an impressive abstraction that only one person understands.

sections.title: Make room for curiosity.
paragraphs: This garden is a place to explore the more playful side of that thinking. Three.js, motion, and interactive systems let me turn otherwise invisible connections into something tangible.
I’m interested in problems that need someone to move comfortably between product questions and implementation detail — and stay with the work through review, release, and the next iteration.

scenarios.title: Request routing & scaling
scenarios.explanation: A router sends work to healthy replicas.
scenarios.why: Availability depends on health signals as well as capacity.
scenarios.tradeoff: More replicas add coordination and operational cost. A modular monolith can keep boundaries clear in one deployment; separate services add independent deployment and network failure modes.

scenarios.title: Data modeling & queries
scenarios.explanation: Choose a relational or document view and trace a lookup.
scenarios.why: Model data around access patterns and consistency needs.
scenarios.tradeoff: Indexes cost storage and writes. Documents simplify some reads; relational constraints make relationships explicit.

scenarios.title: Caching
scenarios.explanation: Read from the source once, then serve a cached value until it expires.
scenarios.why: Avoid repeated source work while making freshness explicit.
scenarios.tradeoff: Cached data can become stale. Expiry and invalidation need deliberate rules.

scenarios.title: Background jobs
scenarios.explanation: Queue a job, retry a failed attempt and suppress duplicate work.
scenarios.why: Long-running work should survive transient failures.
scenarios.tradeoff: Retries can repeat side effects. An idempotency key makes duplicate handling explicit.

scenarios.title: Authentication & authorization
scenarios.explanation: Identify the caller, then check permission to perform an admin action.
scenarios.why: Being signed in is different from being allowed to act.
scenarios.tradeoff: Central policy improves consistency, but permission changes and stale sessions need care.

scenarios.title: Delivery & observability
scenarios.explanation: Follow a change through tests, build, deployment and a traced request.
scenarios.why: Checks and observable outcomes help teams detect and recover from failures.
scenarios.tradeoff: More telemetry costs storage and attention. Keep signals useful and avoid sensitive data in logs.
